content: Acute otitis media (AOM), commonly referred to as an acute middle ear infection, is one of the most prevalent illnesses in children and a leading reason for prescribing antibiotics in this population. Current guidelines often recommend antibiotics as the first-line treatment for severe cases of AOM. However, the widespread use of antibiotics has contributed to the growing problem of antibiotic resistance, making the prevention of AOM episodes a critical priority. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of probiotics in preventing the occurrence of AOM and reducing its severity in children. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, PubMed, and Embase, as well as two trial registries. The search was completed in October 2018, and no restrictions were applied regarding language, publication date, or publication status. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving children up to 18 years of age were included, comparing probiotics with placebo, usual care, or no probiotic intervention. A total of 17 RCTs involving 3,488 children were included in the analysis, with 16 of these trials contributing data to the meta-analyses. The mean age of the children across the studies was 2.4 years. Four trials included children with a mean age of less than 1 year, two trials included children aged between 1 and 2 years, and ten trials included children older than 2 years. The probiotic strains evaluated varied across the studies, with 11 trials investigating Lactobacillus-containing probiotics and six trials evaluating Streptococcus-containing probiotics. The results showed that children receiving probiotics had a lower risk of experiencing one or more episodes of AOM during the treatment period compared to those in the control groups (risk ratio [RR] 0.77, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.63 to 0.93; 16 trials; 2,961 participants). The number needed to treat for an additional beneficial outcome (NNTB) was 10, based on moderate-certainty evidence. A subgroup analysis revealed that among children not prone to otitis media, the use of probiotics was associated with a significantly lower risk of AOM (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.49 to 0.84; 11 trials; 2,227 participants; NNTB = 9; moderate-certainty evidence). However, in children who were prone to otitis media, there was no significant difference between the probiotic and control groups (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.11; 5 trials; 734 participants; high-certainty evidence). The test for subgroup differences was statistically significant (P = 0.007). None of the included trials reported data on the severity of AOM episodes. Additionally, the proportion of children experiencing adverse events did not differ significantly between the probiotic and control groups (odds ratio [OR] 1.54, 95% CI 0.60 to 3.94; 4 trials; 395 participants; low-certainty evidence). Probiotics were found to reduce the proportion of children requiring antibiotics for any type of infection (RR 0.66, 95% CI 0.51 to 0.86; 8 trials; 1,768 participants; NNTB = 8; moderate-certainty evidence). However, subgroup analyses comparing antibiotic use specifically for AOM versus other infections did not reveal significant differences. There was no significant difference between the probiotic and control groups in the mean number of school days missed due to illness (mean difference [MD] −0.95, 95% CI −2.47 to 0.57; 5 trials; 1,280 participants; moderate-certainty evidence). Similarly, compliance with the intervention did not differ between groups (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.99 to 1.05; 5 trials; 990 participants). Probiotics were also associated with a reduction in the proportion of children experiencing other types of infections, such as respiratory or gastrointestinal infections (RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.87; 11 trials; 3,610 participants; NNTB = 12; moderate-certainty evidence). Subgroup analyses for different types of infections did not show significant differences. The studies included in this review exhibited considerable variability in the probiotic strains used, as well as in the dose, frequency, and duration of administration. This heterogeneity likely contributed to the variability in the results. Sensitivity analyses of funnel plots did not indicate publication bias. In conclusion, probiotics may help prevent AOM in children who are not prone to the condition, but the inconsistency observed in subgroup analyses warrants caution in interpreting these findings. Probiotics were also shown to reduce the proportion of children requiring antibiotics for any infection. Importantly, the use of probiotics did not increase the risk of adverse events. However, further research is needed to determine the optimal probiotic strain, dosage, frequency, and duration of administration for preventing AOM in children.
